title: Tartarus. Elysium. Anchises
titleEn: Tartarus, Elysium and Anchises — Aeneid VI.608–702
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Sibyl goes on with her account of Tartarus. Shut in there, waiting for their punishment, are those who hated their brothers while they lived, struck a parent or cheated a client; those who brooded alone over their wealth and set none of it aside for their own people, the largest crowd of all; men killed for adultery; and those who took up arms in an unholy cause and broke faith with their masters. She will not say what each one suffers: some roll a huge rock, some hang stretched on the spokes of wheels; Theseus sits, and will sit for ever; and Phlegyas cries out through the shades, warning all to learn justice and not to scorn the gods. Here is the man who sold his country for gold and set a tyrant over it, the man who made and unmade laws for a price, the man who forced his way into his daughter's bed: all dared a monstrous crime and carried it through, and not a hundred tongues could tell every shape of their crimes or every name of their punishments. Then the Sibyl hurries Aeneas on: she can see the walls of Dis's palace, forged by the Cyclopes, and the gateway where the golden bough is to be left. Aeneas sprinkles himself with fresh water and fixes the bough on the threshold. They come down into Elysium, the joyful homes of the blessed, clothed in a more generous light, with a sun and stars of their own. There the spirits exercise on grassy wrestling-grounds, dance and sing, while Orpheus, the Thracian priest in his long robe, plays the seven notes of his lyre. There is the ancient line of Teucer, the heroes Ilus and Assaracus and Dardanus, the founder of Troy; their arms and empty chariots stand by, their spears are planted in the ground and their horses graze, for the pleasures they had in life go with them below. Others feast and sing a paean in a fragrant laurel grove from which the Eridanus flows: those wounded fighting for their country, priests who kept themselves pure, faithful poets, those who made life richer with their inventions and those whose services earned them remembrance, all with snow-white headbands. The Sibyl asks Musaeus, who stands head and shoulders above the throng, where Anchises is to be found; he answers that none of them has a fixed home, and leads them up a ridge from which they see the shining plains below. Anchises, deep in a green valley, is reviewing the souls who are to rise to the light, among them his own descendants. When he sees Aeneas coming over the grass, he stretches out both hands in tears: his son has come at last, as he had reckoned, after so many lands, seas and dangers, and he had feared what the kingdom of Libya might do to him. Aeneas answers that his father's sad image drove him here, and begs to clasp his hand; three times he tries to put his arms around him, and three times the shade slips through his hands, light as the winds, like a dream on the wing.

sentences.t:
Hic, quibus invisi fratres, dum vita manebat,
pulsatusve parens, et fraus innexa clienti,
aut qui divitiis soli incubuere repertis,
nec partem posuere suis (quae maxima turba est),
sentences.l:
Here those to whom hateful were brothers, while life remained,
or a parent was beaten, and fraud woven against a client,
or who over riches, alone, brooded, once found,
and no share set aside for their own (which is the greatest crowd),
sentences.i: Here are those who hated their brothers while life lasted, or struck a father, or wove a web of fraud about a client; those who sat brooding alone over the wealth they had come by and set no share of it aside for their own (and theirs is the largest crowd of all);
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, but the Sibyl's speech, begun at 562, runs on: having told of the great sinners of myth, she turns to ordinary human crimes. The sentence is a long list of relative clauses whose main verb, 'exspectant', does not come until 614, so it is divided here at a comma. 'Quibus invisi fratres (erant)' is 'to whom brothers were hateful', the dative with 'invisus'; 'dum vita manebat' is 'while life lasted', a phrase that comes again at 661. 'Pulsatusve parens' is 'or (to whom) a parent (was) struck', and 'fraus innexa clienti' 'a fraud woven against a client', 'clienti' a dative. Both were old Roman sacrileges: the client owed his patron loyalty and the patron owed him protection, and the Twelve Tables made the patron who cheated his client 'sacer', forfeit to the gods. 'Incubuere' is 'incubuerunt' (the '-ere' perfect again), 'lay upon', the picture of a dragon couched on its hoard; 'soli' is 'alone', keeping it to themselves, and 'repertis' is 'found', 'come by'. 'Nec partem posuere suis' is 'and set aside no share for their own (kin)'. The parenthesis 'quae maxima turba est' is the Sibyl's dry remark, 'and that is the biggest crowd'.

sentences.t:
quique ob adulterium caesi, quique arma secuti
impia nec veriti dominorum fallere dextras,
inclusi poenam exspectant.
sentences.l:
and those who for adultery were slain, and who arms followed
unholy, nor feared of their masters to cheat the right hands,
shut in, their punishment await.
sentences.i: those killed for adultery; and those who followed an unholy cause in arms and did not shrink from breaking faith with their masters: all are shut in here, waiting for their punishment.
sentences.n: 'Quique… quique' is 'and those who… and those who', still the list of the guilty. 'Ob adulterium caesi (sunt)' is 'were slain for adultery': Roman law let a husband or father kill an adulterer caught in the act, and the dead man still pays below. 'Arma… impia' runs over the line-end, 'unholy arms'. 'Dominorum fallere dextras' is 'to cheat the right hands of their masters': the right hand is the pledge of faith, so this is to break faith with a master. It is usually taken of slaves who deserted their masters to fight in the civil wars of Virgil's own time, as many did for Sextus Pompeius. 'Veriti' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'vereor', 'having feared', here 'not shrinking'. At last the main verb: 'inclusi poenam exspectant', 'shut in, they wait for their punishment'.

sentences.t:
Ne quaere doceri
quam poenam, aut quae forma viros fortunave mersit.
sentences.l:
Do not seek to be taught
what punishment, or what shape or fortune has sunk the men.
sentences.i: Do not ask to be told what punishment awaits them, or what shape of doom or turn of fortune has drowned them.
sentences.n: 'Ne quaere' is 'ne' with the imperative, a poetic prohibition, 'do not seek'; prose would say 'noli quaerere' or 'ne quaesieris'. 'Doceri' is a present passive infinitive, 'to be taught'. 'Quam poenam (exspectent)' is an indirect question with its verb left out. 'Forma' is 'shape', 'kind', the kind of punishment; 'fortunave' is 'or fortune', and 'mersit' agrees with the nearer subject: 'what form or fate has sunk (drowned) the men'. The Sibyl is saying the tale would never end, as she will say again at 625.

sentences.t:
Saxum ingens volvunt alii, radiisque rotarum
districti pendent;
sentences.l:
A rock huge roll some, and on the spokes of wheels
stretched out they hang;
sentences.i: Some roll a huge rock; others hang spread out on the spokes of wheels;
sentences.n: 'Alii' is 'some'; the second group is understood from 'pendent', 'others hang'. The rock and the wheel are the punishments of Sisyphus, who rolls a stone up a hill for ever only to see it roll down (Odyssey 11.593–600), and of Ixion, bound to a turning wheel; Virgil lets them stand as types, without names, for whoever has deserved them. 'Radiis rotarum' is 'on the spokes of wheels'. 'Districti' is 'stretched apart', 'pulled taut', the limbs spread on the spokes.

sentences.t:
sedet, aeternumque sedebit,
infelix Theseus;
sentences.l:
sits, and forever will sit,
unhappy Theseus;
sentences.i: luckless Theseus sits there, and will go on sitting for all time;
sentences.n: 'Sedet… sedebit' sets the present beside the future: he sits now and always will. 'Aeternum' is an adverbial accusative, 'for ever'. Theseus went down with Pirithous to carry off Proserpina (Charon recalls the attempt at 392–397); in one story the two were fastened to a rock seat in Hades. Other stories have Hercules set Theseus free; here Virgil keeps him below for ever, though at 122 Aeneas named him among those who had made the journey. 'Infelix' is 'unlucky', 'ill-starred', and is thrown forward to the head of the line. 'Theseus' is two syllables, Thē-seus, the Greek diphthong eu.

sentences.t:
Phlegyasque miserrimus omnis
admonet, et magna testatur voce per umbras:
sentences.l:
and Phlegyas, most wretched, all
admonishes, and with great voice bears witness through the shades:
sentences.i: and Phlegyas in his utter misery warns every one of them, proclaiming in a great voice through the shadows:
sentences.n: In the story Servius tells, Phlegyas, father of Coronis (and in some accounts of Ixion), set fire to Apollo's temple at Delphi after the god seduced his daughter, and was cast into Tartarus for it. 'Miserrimus' is a superlative, 'most wretched'. 'Omnis' is Greenough's accusative plural in '-is' for 'omnes' (you'll see this constantly), the object of 'admonet', 'warns all'. 'Testatur' is a deponent, 'calls to witness', 'declares solemnly'. The colon introduces his cry.

sentences.t: “Discite iustitiam moniti, et non temnere divos.
sentences.l: ‘Learn justice, being warned, and not to despise the gods.’
sentences.i: ‘Take warning, all of you: learn to be just, and learn not to hold the gods in contempt.’
sentences.n: Phlegyas's cry, a single line set inside the Sibyl's speech; it is given here in single marks. Greenough prints an opening mark before 'Discite' and none to close it: the only closing mark in the passage, at 627, ends the Sibyl's speech. We take Phlegyas's words to be this line alone, as most editors do, with the Sibyl speaking again from 621: the 'Non… possim' of 625–627 is plainly her own voice, answering her 'Ne quaere doceri' of 614. Some have run his words on further, and the print does not decide it, so t is left as printed. 'Discite' is a plural imperative, 'learn', governing both 'iustitiam', 'justice', and the infinitive 'non temnere divos', 'not to despise the gods'. 'Moniti' is a perfect participle, 'having been warned' (by my fate). The line recalls Pindar, who has Ixion on his wheel tell mortals to repay a benefactor with kindness (Pythian 2.21–24). 'Divos' is 'deos', 'the gods'.

sentences.t:
Vendidit hic auro patriam, dominumque potentem
imposuit;
sentences.l:
Sold this one for gold his country, and a master powerful
imposed;
sentences.i: This one sold his country for gold and set a tyrant over it;
sentences.n: The Sibyl again. 'Hic… hic' is 'this one… that one', pointing at the sinners as if they stood before her. 'Auro' is an ablative of price, 'for gold'. 'Dominum… potentem' runs over the line-end, 'a powerful master', a tyrant over a free people, and 'imposuit' is 'set over (it)'. The poet names no one; Servius, the ancient commentator, thought of Curio, said to have sold himself to Julius Caesar.

sentences.t: fixit leges pretio atque refixit;
sentences.l: he posted laws for a price and unposted them;
sentences.i: another set up laws for a bribe and for a bribe took them down;
sentences.n: Roman laws were engraved on bronze tablets and nailed up ('figere') in public; 'refigere' is to take them down, so to repeal them. 'Pretio' is an ablative of price, 'for money', and goes with both verbs. Servius thought of Mark Antony, who was accused of posting laws, as if from Caesar's papers, for whoever would pay.

sentences.t: hic thalamum invasit natae vetitosque hymenaeos;
sentences.l: this one invaded the bedchamber of his daughter and a forbidden marriage;
sentences.i: this one broke into his own daughter's bedchamber, into a marriage that was forbidden;
sentences.n: 'Thalamum… natae' is 'his daughter's bedchamber': 'thalamus' is the marriage-chamber, and 'invasit' is 'forced his way into', 'seized'. 'Vetitos… hymenaeos' is 'forbidden marriages', the plural for the singular; Hymen, or Hymenaeus, was the Greek god of weddings, and 'hymenaeus' becomes a word for marriage itself. Greek myth knew such crimes (Thyestes and his daughter Pelopia, for one); the Sibyl names no names, and the line says no more than this.

sentences.t: ausi omnes immane nefas, ausoque potiti.
sentences.l: they dared, all, a monstrous wrong, and of what they dared they possessed themselves.
sentences.i: every one of them dared some unspeakable outrage, and saw his daring through.
sentences.n: 'Ausi (sunt)' is the perfect of the semi-deponent 'audeo', 'they dared'; 'omnes' is the subject. 'Nefas' is an indeclinable noun, 'an unspeakable wrong', a crime against divine law, and 'immane' agrees with it, 'monstrous'. 'Auso… potiti' is 'having got possession of the thing dared': 'potior' takes the ablative, and 'auso' is the perfect participle of 'audeo' used as a noun. The sting is that they succeeded: their crimes were not just attempted, they were done.

sentences.t:
Non, mihi si linguae centum sint oraque centum,
ferrea vox, omnis scelerum comprendere formas,
omnia poenarum percurrere nomina possim.”
sentences.l:
No, if I had tongues a hundred and mouths a hundred,
a voice of iron, all the forms of crimes to take in,
all the names of punishments to run through, I could not.”
sentences.i: No: were I given a hundred tongues and as many mouths, and a voice of iron, even so I could not compass every form their crimes have taken, nor tell over every name of their punishments.”
sentences.n: The closing mark ends the Sibyl's long speech (562–627). 'Si… sint… possim' is a condition with the present subjunctive in both halves, the 'should… would' kind: 'if I should have, I would not be able'. 'Mihi… sint' is a dative of possession, 'there should be to me', 'I should have'. 'Ferrea vox' is a third item, with 'sit' understood. 'Omnis… formas' is Greenough's '-is' accusative plural again; 'comprendere' is the contracted form of 'comprehendere', 'to take in', 'to sum up', and 'percurrere' is 'to run through', 'to list'. The figure is Homer's: before the Catalogue of Ships he says he could not name the multitude even with ten tongues, ten mouths and a heart of bronze (Iliad 2.488–490). Virgil had already used the hundred tongues and iron voice in the Georgics (2.43–44).

sentences.i: When the long-lived priestess of Phoebus had said this, she went on: “But now, come, be on your way and complete the task you have undertaken; let us hurry,” she said;
sentences.n: The print has 'munus; / “adceleremus ait; Cyclopum', a misprint for 'munus; / adceleremus” ait; “Cyclopum': an opening mark for the closing mark after 'adceleremus', and no opening mark before 'Cyclopum' (the same slip as at 6.46 and 6.52). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i give the reading. A new paragraph. 'Haec ubi dicta dedit' is 'when she had given these words', 'dicta dare' being a poetic way of saying 'speak'. 'Longaeva', 'long-lived', fits the Sibyl, who was said to have been granted as many years as grains of sand in her hand. 'Sed iam age' is 'but come now', 'age' an interjection from the imperative of 'ago'. 'Carpe viam' is 'take the road', literally 'pluck' or 'seize' it. 'Susceptum… munus' is 'the task undertaken', and 'munus' is also 'gift': the duty is to deliver the golden bough. 'Adceleremus' is Greenough's spelling of 'acceleremus', a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us hasten'.

sentences.t:
Cyclopum educta caminis
moenia conspicio atque adverso fornice portas,
haec ubi nos praecepta iubent deponere dona.”
sentences.l:
“the walls brought out in the Cyclopes' furnaces
I see, and with arch facing us the gates,
where our instructions bid us lay down these gifts.”
sentences.i: “I can make out the walls that the Cyclopes' furnaces brought forth, and the gateway with its arch facing us, where we are bidden to lay down this gift.”
sentences.n: The second half of the Sibyl's words (see the note on the previous unit). 'Cyclopum educta caminis… moenia' is 'the walls brought up out of the furnaces of the Cyclopes': the Cyclopes here are the smiths who work Vulcan's forges (they are seen at work in Book VIII), and the palace walls of Dis are of forged metal. 'Educta' is 'drawn out', 'raised'. 'Adverso fornice' is an ablative of description, 'with arch facing (us)'. 'Ubi' is 'where', referring back to the gates, and 'haec… dona', 'these gifts', spans the line. 'Praecepta' are the instructions she gave Aeneas when the bough was first named (136–148): it is Proserpina's gift. 'Dona' is a plural for the single gift.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et pariter, gressi per opaca viarum,
corripiunt spatium medium, foribusque propinquant.
sentences.l:
She had spoken, and side by side, stepping through the darkness of the ways,
they hurry over the space between, and to the doors draw near.
sentences.i: She had finished, and together they went on through the dark ways, quickly crossed the distance between, and came close to the doors.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is a pluperfect, 'she had spoken', a common way of closing a speech and moving on. 'Pariter' is 'side by side', 'together'. 'Gressi' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'gradior', 'having stepped'. 'Opaca viarum' is a neuter plural adjective with a genitive, 'the dark (parts) of the ways', a Greek-style turn for 'the dark ways', like 'strata viarum' at 1.422. 'Corripiunt spatium medium' is 'they snatch up the space between', that is, they cover it quickly. 'Foribus' is a dative with 'propinquant', 'draw near to the doors'.

sentences.t:
Occupat Aeneas aditum, corpusque recenti
spargit aqua, ramumque adverso in limine figit.
sentences.l:
Takes Aeneas the entrance, and his body with fresh
sprinkles water, and the bough on the threshold facing him fixes.
sentences.i: Aeneas took his stand in the entrance, sprinkled his body with fresh water, and set up the bough on the threshold that faced him.
sentences.n: 'Occupat' is 'takes possession of', 'gets to first': he steps into the entrance. 'Recenti… aqua' frames the next line's verb, 'with fresh water', running water from a spring: he purifies himself after passing so near the place of the guilty, before going on to the blessed and presenting the gift. 'Ramum… figit' is 'fixes the bough' on the threshold, an offering hung up for the goddess, as worshippers fixed gifts to a temple door. 'Adverso in limine' is 'on the threshold opposite', 'facing him'.

sentences.t:
His demum exactis, perfecto munere divae,
devenere locos laetos et amoena virecta
fortunatorum nemorum sedesque beatas.
sentences.l:
These things at last carried out, the service to the goddess performed,
they came down to the joyful places and the pleasant green lawns
of the fortunate groves, and the blessed seats.
sentences.i: When at last this was done and the goddess had her due, they came down into the places of gladness, the lovely green lawns of the woods of the fortunate, the homes of the blessed.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the arrival in Elysium. 'His demum exactis' and 'perfecto munere divae' are two ablatives absolute, 'these things finally finished, the goddess's service completed'; the 'diva' is Proserpina, and 'munus' is again both the duty and the gift. 'Devenere' is 'devenerunt', 'they came down to'. 'Amoena virecta' are 'pleasant green places', lawns; 'amoenus' is the word for a delightful landscape. 'Fortunatorum nemorum' is 'of the groves of the fortunate', recalling the Islands of the Blest (the 'fortunatae insulae'), and 'sedes beatas' is 'the seats of the blessed'. Homer puts the Elysian plain at the end of the earth (Odyssey 4.563–568); Virgil places it below, within the realm of Dis.

sentences.t:
Largior hic campos aether et lumine vestit
purpureo, solemque suum, sua sidera norunt.
sentences.l:
More bountiful here the air is, and the plains it clothes with light
bright-hued, and their own sun, their own stars they know.
sentences.i: Here the air is more open-handed and dresses the fields in radiant light; they know their own sun, their own stars.
sentences.n: 'Largior… aether' is 'a more lavish upper air': 'largior' is best taken as a predicate with 'est' understood, and 'et' joins it to 'vestit', 'the air here is ampler, and clothes the fields with light', 'lumine… purpureo' running over the line-end. 'Purpureus' in poetry is less 'purple' than 'radiant', 'glowing', any rich bright colour. 'Norunt' is the shortened form of 'noverunt', 'they know', a perfect with present sense. 'Solem suum, sua sidera' is 'their own sun, their own stars': Elysium has a sky of its own, apart from ours, as Pindar says the sun shines below for the blessed while it is night here.

sentences.t:
Pars in gramineis exercent membra palaestris,
contendunt ludo et fulva luctantur harena;
sentences.l:
Some on grassy wrestling-grounds exercise their limbs,
vie in sport, and wrestle on the tawny sand;
sentences.i: Some train their bodies on wrestling-floors of grass, vie with one another in sport, and wrestle on the tawny sand;
sentences.n: 'Pars… exercent' is a singular collective noun with a plural verb, agreement by sense: 'part (of them) exercise'. 'Palaestris' are wrestling-schools, open exercise-grounds; here they are grassy. 'Contendunt ludo' is 'contend in sport', and 'fulva… harena' is 'on the tawny sand', the sanded floor of the wrestling-ring. The blessed keep up the pastimes they loved in life, as the next lines say outright (653–655).

sentences.t: pars pedibus plaudunt choreas et carmina dicunt.
sentences.l: some with their feet beat out dances and recite songs.
sentences.i: others beat out a dance with their feet and recite their verses.
sentences.n: 'Pars… pars' is 'some… others'. 'Pedibus plaudunt choreas' is 'beat out dances with their feet', 'choreas' a kind of cognate object; 'plaudo' is to strike or clap, here the stamp of feet keeping time. 'Carmina dicunt' is 'they recite songs', 'dicere' being the usual verb for performing a poem, sung or chanted, at the dance.

sentences.t:
Nec non Threïcius longa cum veste sacerdos
obloquitur numeris septem discrimina vocum,
iamque eadem digitis, iam pectine pulsat eburno.
sentences.l:
And also the Thracian, in long robe, the priest
sounds in answer to the measures the seven distinctions of notes,
and now them with fingers, now with ivory quill strikes.
sentences.i: Nor is the Thracian priest missing: in his long robe he answers their rhythms with the seven distinct notes of his lyre, sounding them sometimes with his fingers, sometimes with a plectrum of ivory.
sentences.n: 'Nec non' is 'and also', a double negative making a positive. 'Threïcius… sacerdos', 'the Thracian priest', is Orpheus, the singer of Thrace, son of the Muse Calliope; Aeneas named him in his prayer to the Sibyl (6.119–120), as the man who went down to fetch his wife. He is a priest as founder of mysteries, and the 'longa… vestis' is the long robe of a professional lyre-player. Greenough's diaeresis on 'Threïcius' marks a separate syllable, Thre-ï-ci-us, as in the Greek 'Threikios'. 'Obloquitur numeris' is 'sounds in answer to the measures', accompanying the rhythm of the dancers. 'Septem discrimina vocum' is 'the seven distinct notes', the strings of the seven-stringed lyre. 'Eadem' is neuter plural, 'the same (notes)'. 'Pectine… eburno' is 'with an ivory plectrum', the pick the player held.

sentences.t:
Hic genus antiquum Teucri, pulcherrima proles,
magnanimi heroes, nati melioribus annis,
Ilusque Assaracusque et Troiae Dardanus auctor.
sentences.l:
Here the ancient race of Teucer, most beautiful offspring,
great-hearted heroes, born in better years,
both Ilus and Assaracus and of Troy Dardanus the founder.
sentences.i: Here is the ancient line of Teucer, a race of surpassing beauty, great-hearted heroes born in a better age, Ilus and Assaracus, and Dardanus, the founder of Troy.
sentences.n: The verb 'sunt' is understood: 'here (are)'. 'Genus antiquum Teucri' is 'the ancient race of Teucer', the first king of the Troad, whose daughter married Dardanus; so the Trojans are 'Teucri', Teucrians. 'Nati melioribus annis' is 'born in better years', the age of heroes. Ilus founded Ilium (Troy's other name) and was the grandfather of Priam; his brother Assaracus was the great-grandfather of Aeneas, through Capys and Anchises; Dardanus, son of Jupiter, came from Italy and founded the line, so Aeneas's journey to Italy is a homecoming (3.167). 'Ilusque Assaracusque' is the double '-que', 'both… and', and 'auctor' is 'founder'.

sentences.t: Arma procul currusque virum miratur inanes.
sentences.l: Their arms at a distance and the chariots of the men he wonders at, empty.
sentences.i: Aeneas gazes in wonder at their arms set some way off, and at the heroes' empty chariots.
sentences.n: The subject of 'miratur' is Aeneas. 'Procul' is 'at a distance', not far away but set apart. 'Virum' is the old genitive plural, 'virorum', 'of the men'. 'Inanes' is held to the end of the line, 'empty', unmanned or insubstantial, phantom chariots; it goes with 'currus' (and the Latin Library's 'inanis' is the same word in the other spelling of the accusative plural).

sentences.t:
Stant terra defixae hastae, passimque soluti
per campum pascuntur equi.
sentences.l:
Stand in the earth fixed spears, and everywhere unyoked
over the plain graze the horses.
sentences.i: Their spears stand planted in the ground, and their horses, loosed from the yoke, graze all over the plain.
sentences.n: 'Stant… defixae hastae' is 'spears stand fixed', 'terra' an ablative of place, 'in the ground'. A spear stuck upright in the earth is a sign of rest from battle. 'Passim' is 'here and there', 'everywhere'. 'Soluti' is 'loosed', unharnessed from the chariots. 'Stant' opens the line: a still picture.

sentences.t:
Quae gratia currum
armorumque fuit vivis, quae cura nitentis
pascere equos, eadem sequitur tellure repostos.
sentences.l:
What delight in chariots
and arms there was for them living, what care to pasture sleek
horses, the same follows them laid in the earth.
sentences.i: The pleasure they took in chariots and arms while they lived, their concern to feed glossy horses, goes with them still, now they are laid in the earth.
sentences.n: 'Quae gratia… eadem' is 'what delight… the same (delight)', a relative clause standing before its antecedent. 'Currum' is the contracted genitive plural of 'currus', for 'curruum', 'of chariots'. 'Vivis' is a dative, 'for (them) living'. 'Quae cura… pascere' is 'what concern to feed', with the infinitive. 'Nitentis… equos' is 'gleaming horses', Greenough's '-is' accusative plural. 'Repostos' is a syncopated 'repositos', 'laid away', 'buried'; 'tellure' is 'in the earth'. The thought is Homer's, whose shades keep their earthly character (Odyssey 11, where Orion still hunts and Achilles still asks after his son).

sentences.t:
Conspicit, ecce, alios dextra laevaque per herbam
vescentis, laetumque choro paeana canentis
inter odoratum lauri nemus, unde superne
plurimus Eridani per silvam volvitur amnis.
sentences.l:
He sees, look, others on the right and left over the grass
feasting, and a joyful paean in chorus singing,
amid a fragrant grove of laurel, from where upward
the full stream of Eridanus through the wood rolls.
sentences.i: And see, to his right and left he notices others eating on the grass and singing a glad paean as one choir, amid a sweet-scented grove of laurel, from where the Eridanus pours its full stream up through the woods toward the world above.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ecce', 'look!', brings the reader into Aeneas's view. 'Vescentis' and 'canentis' are Greenough's '-is' accusative plurals, agreeing with 'alios'; 'vescor' is 'to feed', 'to feast'. 'Paeana' is a Greek accusative, 'a paean', a hymn of thanksgiving to Apollo, and the laurel is Apollo's tree. 'Odoratum' is 'fragrant'; the Latin Library's 'lauris' for 'lauri' does not change the sense. 'Unde' is 'from where'. 'Superne' is disputed: many take it as 'upward', the river rising here and flowing to the world above, since the Po (the Eridanus) was thought to have an underground source; others take it as 'from above'. 'Plurimus' is 'most abundant', 'in full flood', with 'amnis'.

sentences.t:
Hic manus ob patriam pugnando volnera passi,
quique sacerdotes casti, dum vita manebat,
quique pii vates et Phoebo digna locuti,
sentences.l:
Here the band who for their country, fighting, suffered wounds,
and those who were priests pure, while life remained,
and who were faithful bards and spoke things worthy of Phoebus,
sentences.i: Here is the company of those who took wounds fighting for their country, those who were priests and kept themselves pure while life lasted, those who were faithful poets and spoke what was worthy of Phoebus,
sentences.n: Another long list with its main verb at the end (665), divided here at a comma. 'Manus' is 'a band', a collective noun followed by the plural 'passi', agreement by sense: 'a band (of men) who suffered'. 'Ob patriam pugnando' is 'by fighting for their country', 'pugnando' the ablative of the gerund. 'Volnera' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera'. 'Quique… quique' is 'and those who… and those who', with 'erant' understood. 'Sacerdotes casti' are priests who kept their vows of purity, and 'dum vita manebat' repeats the phrase of 608, now of the good. 'Vates' is both prophet and poet, and 'pii vates' are poets true to their calling; 'Phoebo digna' is 'things worthy of Phoebus', Apollo, god of poetry.

sentences.t:
inventas aut qui vitam excoluere per artes,
quique sui memores alios fecere merendo,
omnibus his nivea cinguntur tempora vitta.
sentences.l:
or who life refined through arts discovered,
and who made others mindful of them by deserving well:
of all these with a snowy fillet are bound the temples.
sentences.i: those who enriched life by the arts they discovered, and those whose good deeds made others remember them: all these have their brows bound with a snow-white headband.
sentences.n: 'Inventas… per artes' is 'through arts discovered', the inventors who 'excoluere vitam', 'refined', 'civilized life' ('excoluere' is 'excoluerunt'). 'Sui memores alios fecere merendo' is 'made others mindful of them by deserving (well)', 'merendo' the ablative of the gerund; 'sui' is the genitive of the reflexive with 'memores'. The Latin Library has 'aliquos', 'some (people)', for Greenough's 'alios', 'others': a small difference, 'made some remember them' against 'made other people remember them'. 'Omnibus his' resumes the whole list, a dative of reference: 'for all these the temples are bound'. 'Tempora' are the temples of the head. The 'vitta', a woollen headband, was the mark of a priest or a consecrated person; 'nivea' is 'snow-white'.

sentences.t:
Quos circumfusos sic est adfata Sybilla,
Musaeum ante omnes, medium nam plurima turba
hunc habet, atque umeris exstantem suspicit altis:
sentences.l:
Them, poured around, thus addressed the Sibyl,
Musaeus before all; for in the middle the great throng
holds him, and looks up at him standing out with his tall shoulders:
sentences.i: As they flocked round her, the Sibyl spoke to them, and to Musaeus above all, for he stood in the middle of the great throng, which looked up at him as he rose head and shoulders above them:
sentences.n: The print has 'Sybilla', a misprint for 'Sibylla' (the edition prints 'Sibylla' everywhere else, eleven times with its other cases); t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i give the reading. A new paragraph. 'Quos' is a connecting relative, 'and them'. 'Circumfusos' is 'poured round', 'crowding around'. 'Est adfata' is the perfect of the deponent 'adfor' ('affor'), 'addressed'. 'Musaeum ante omnes' is 'Musaeus before all', also governed by 'adfata est'. Musaeus was a legendary singer of Attica, called a pupil or son of Orpheus and linked with the mysteries of Eleusis. 'Medium… hunc habet' is 'holds him in the middle'; 'plurima turba' is 'the very great crowd'. 'Umeris exstantem… altis' is 'standing out with his tall shoulders', 'taller by the shoulders', a hero's height.

sentences.t:
“Dicite, felices animae, tuque, optime vates,
quae regio Anchisen, quis habet locus?
sentences.l:
“Tell, happy souls, and you, best of bards,
what region Anchises, what place holds?
sentences.i: “Tell us, blessed spirits, and you, finest of poets, what quarter, what place is Anchises' home?
sentences.n: The Sibyl's question opens. 'Felices animae' is a vocative, 'happy souls', and 'optime vates' is Musaeus, 'best of poets'. 'Quae regio… quis… locus' are two interrogatives with the one verb 'habet', 'what region, what place holds (him)'. 'Anchisen' is a Greek accusative of 'Anchises'.

sentences.t:
Illius ergo
venimus, et magnos Erebi transnavimus amnes.”
sentences.l:
For his sake
we have come, and the great rivers of Erebus have sailed across.”
sentences.i: It is for his sake that we have come and crossed the great rivers of Erebus.”
sentences.n: 'Illius ergo' is 'for his sake': 'ergo' with a preceding genitive is an old formal use, 'on account of', found in laws and religious language. 'Erebi' is 'of Erebus', the darkness of the underworld. 'Transnavimus' is 'we have sailed across', in Charon's boat (the Latin Library's 'tranavimus' is the same verb with a shorter prefix). The closing mark ends the Sibyl's words.

sentences.t: Atque huic responsum paucis ita reddidit heros:
sentences.l: And to her an answer in few words thus returned the hero:
sentences.i: And the hero gave her this brief reply:
sentences.n: 'Huic' is 'to her', the Sibyl. 'Paucis' is 'in few (words)', with 'verbis' understood. 'Responsum… reddidit' is 'gave back an answer'. 'Heros' is Musaeus: the word is used of any great man of the heroic age, singers included.

sentences.t: “Nulli certa domus;
sentences.l: “To none a fixed home;
sentences.i: “None of us has a settled home;
sentences.n: 'Nulli certa domus (est)' is a dative of possession, 'to no one is there a fixed home'. The blessed wander freely; there are no allotted houses in Elysium.

sentences.t:
lucis habitamus opacis,
riparumque toros et prata recentia rivis
incolimus.
sentences.l:
in shady groves we dwell,
and the couches of banks and meadows fresh with streams
we inhabit.
sentences.i: we haunt the shadowy woods, and keep to the soft couches of the riverbanks and the meadows kept fresh by running streams.
sentences.n: 'Lucis… opacis' is 'in shady groves', 'lucus' being a grove, often sacred. 'Riparum toros' is 'the couches of the banks', the soft raised turf along the rivers, on which they recline as on dining-couches. 'Prata recentia rivis' is 'meadows fresh with streams', 'rivis' an ablative of cause. 'Incolimus' is held over to the next line, 'we inhabit'.

sentences.t:
Sed vos, si fert ita corde voluntas,
hoc superate iugum;
sentences.l:
But you, if so carries you in your heart your will,
climb over this ridge;
sentences.i: But if that is your heart's desire, climb this ridge;
sentences.n: 'Si fert ita corde voluntas' is 'if your will carries you so in your heart', a polite formula, 'if you so wish'. 'Superate' is a plural imperative, 'get over', 'climb'. 'Iugum' is a ridge or hilltop.

sentences.t: et facili iam tramite sistam.”
sentences.l: and by an easy path soon I will set you down.”
sentences.i: and I will soon set you down by an easy track where you wish to be.”
sentences.n: 'Facili… tramite' is 'by an easy path', an ablative of way. 'Sistam' is 'I will set (you)', 'place you' where you want to be, with 'vos' understood. The closing mark ends Musaeus's words.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et ante tulit gressum, camposque nitentis
desuper ostentat;
sentences.l:
He spoke, and ahead carried his step, and the plains shining
from above he shows;
sentences.i: He spoke, and walked on ahead of them, and from the height showed them the shining plains;
sentences.n: 'Ante tulit gressum' is 'carried his step ahead', 'went in front'. 'Camposque nitentis' is 'the shining plains', Greenough's '-is' accusative plural again. 'Desuper' is 'from above', from the ridge, and 'ostentat' is 'points out', 'displays'.

sentences.t: dehinc summa cacumina linquunt.
sentences.l: then the topmost peaks they leave.
sentences.i: then they leave the summit of the ridge behind.
sentences.n: 'Dehinc' is 'then', 'next', here pronounced as one syllable. 'Summa cacumina' is 'the topmost peaks', the top of the ridge; 'linquunt' is 'they leave', as they go down into the valley.

sentences.t:
At pater Anchises penitus convalle virenti
inclusas animas superumque ad lumen ituras
lustrabat studio recolens, omnemque suorum
forte recensebat numerum carosque nepotes,
fataque fortunasque virum moresque manusque.
sentences.l:
But father Anchises, deep within a green valley,
the souls shut in and about to go to the light above
was surveying with eagerness, going over them, and the whole of his own
by chance was reviewing number, and his dear descendants,
and the fates and fortunes of the men, and their characters and their deeds.
sentences.i: Father Anchises, meanwhile, far down in a green hollow, was intently surveying the souls shut away there, who were destined to rise to the daylight of the world above, and going over them in his mind; and as it happened he was counting over the whole number of his own line, his beloved descendants, the fates and fortunes of those men, their characters and their deeds.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the turn to Anchises. 'Penitus' is 'deep within'. 'Inclusas animas' is 'the souls enclosed (there)'. 'Superum… lumen' is 'the light above': 'superum' here is the neuter adjective 'superus' agreeing with 'lumen', not the old genitive plural it looks like. 'Ituras' is the future participle of 'eo', 'about to go': these souls are waiting to be born, and Anchises will show them to Aeneas later in this book. 'Lustrabat' is 'was surveying'; 'studio' is 'with zeal', and 'recolens' is 'going over again (in his mind)'. 'Recensebat' is 'was reviewing', 'counting over', as a censor reviews the citizens. 'Nepotes' is 'grandsons', 'descendants'. The last line is a run of four nouns each with '-que': 'fataque fortunasque… moresque manusque', 'fates and fortunes, characters and hands', 'manus' standing for deeds done by hand; 'virum' is the old genitive plural, 'of the men'.

sentences.t:
Isque ubi tendentem adversum per gramina videt
Aenean, alacris palmas utrasque tetendit,
effusaeque genis lacrimae, et vox excidit ore:
sentences.l:
And he, when coming towards him across the grass he saw
Aeneas, eagerly his palms both stretched out,
and poured from his cheeks the tears, and a voice fell from his mouth:
sentences.i: When he caught sight of Aeneas making his way across the grass to meet him, he reached out both hands in his eagerness; tears poured down his cheeks, and his voice burst from his lips:
sentences.n: The print has 'videt', a misprint for 'vidit': the present 'vĭdet' has a short first syllable and cannot stand in the sixth foot, which only the perfect 'vīdit' fills (the Latin Library prints 'vidit'); t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i give the reading. 'Isque' is 'and he', Anchises. 'Tendentem adversum' is 'making his way towards (him)', 'adversum' an adverb or adjective, 'facing'. 'Aenean' is a Greek accusative, held over to the next line. 'Vidit' is the perfect, 'saw'. 'Alacris' is the masculine nominative of 'alacer', 'eager', in the '-is' form Virgil uses. 'Palmas utrasque tetendit' is 'stretched out both his palms', the gesture of greeting and longing; 'utrasque' is plural because each hand is one of a pair. 'Effusae (sunt)… lacrimae' is 'tears poured out', 'genis' an ablative, 'from his cheeks'. 'Excidit ore' is 'fell from his mouth'.

sentences.t:
“Venisti tandem, tuaque exspectata parenti
vicit iter durum pietas?
sentences.l:
“Have you come at last, and your devotion, awaited by your father,
has it overcome the hard road?
sentences.i: “Have you come at last? Has your loyalty, so long awaited by your father, won through the hardships of the road?
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, and Anchises's speech opens. 'Venisti' is the perfect, 'you have come', and the question is close to an exclamation. 'Tua… pietas' frames the clause: 'your sense of duty', Aeneas's love and loyalty to his father. 'Exspectata parenti' is 'awaited by your parent', 'parenti' a dative of the agent with the perfect participle. 'Vicit iter durum' is 'has conquered the hard journey'.

sentences.t:
Datur ora tueri,
nate, tua, et notas audire et reddere voces?
sentences.l:
Is it granted the face to look on,
son, yours, and familiar voices to hear and to give back?
sentences.i: Am I allowed to look on your face, my son, and to hear the voice I know and answer it?
sentences.n: 'Datur' is impersonal, 'is it granted', with three infinitives: 'tueri', 'to look on' (deponent), 'audire' and 'reddere'. 'Ora… tua' frames 'nate', a vocative, 'son'; 'ora' is a plural for the face. 'Notas… voces' are 'well-known voices', 'words', and 'reddere' is 'to give back', to answer: true conversation, which the shades in Homer can rarely have.

sentences.t:
Sic equidem ducebam animo rebarque futurum,
tempora dinumerans, nec me mea cura fefellit.
sentences.l:
So indeed I was reckoning in mind and thought it would be,
counting the times, and has not me my anxious care deceived.
sentences.i: This is how I reckoned it in my mind and believed it would come, counting off the days, and my anxious watching has not played me false.
sentences.n: 'Sic' is 'so', 'thus'. 'Ducebam animo' is 'I was reckoning in my mind', 'ducere' being 'to calculate', 'to reckon'. 'Rebar' is the imperfect of the deponent 'reor', 'I thought', with 'futurum (esse)', 'that it would be'. 'Tempora dinumerans' is 'counting out the times', the days till his coming. 'Cura' is 'care', 'anxious love'; 'fefellit' is the perfect of 'fallo', 'deceived'.

sentences.t:
Quas ego te terras et quanta per aequora vectum
accipio!
sentences.l:
Over what lands, you, and through how great seas carried,
I receive!
sentences.i: Over what lands, across what vast seas you have been carried, and now I welcome you!
sentences.n: An exclamation. 'Quas… terras et quanta per aequora' is 'through what lands and across how great seas': 'per' stands with the second phrase but governs both. 'Te… vectum' is 'you carried', 'vectum' the perfect participle of 'veho'. 'Accipio' is 'I receive', 'I welcome', placed last and alone after the long build-up: 'after what lands and seas I welcome you!'

sentences.t: quantis iactatum, nate, periclis!
sentences.l: by how great dangers tossed, son!
sentences.i: and what dangers, my son, have tossed you about!
sentences.n: 'Quantis… periclis' is 'by how great dangers', an ablative of means; 'periclis' is the shortened form of 'periculis'. 'Iactatum' agrees with 'te' in the line before, 'tossed', 'buffeted', a word used of Aeneas from the first lines of the poem (1.3, 'iactatus'). 'Nate' is a vocative again.

sentences.t: Quam metui, ne quid Libyae tibi regna nocerent!”
sentences.l: How I feared lest anything the realms of Libya might harm you!”
sentences.i: How I dreaded that the realm of Libya might somehow injure you!”
sentences.n: 'Quam metui' is 'how I feared'. 'Ne quid… nocerent' is a clause of fearing: after a verb of fearing 'ne' means 'that' (I feared that…). 'Quid' is 'in any way', an adverbial accusative, and 'noceo' takes the dative 'tibi'. 'Libyae… regna' is Dido's kingdom at Carthage: Anchises's spirit knows of it, as his ghost had urged Aeneas to leave (4.351–353). The closing mark ends his speech.

sentences.t:
Ille autem: “Tua me, genitor, tua tristis imago,
saepius occurrens, haec limina tendere adegit:
sentences.l:
He then: “Your image, father, your sad image,
often meeting me, to make for these thresholds drove:
sentences.i: And Aeneas answered: “It was your image, father, your sorrowful image, coming before me again and again, that drove me to make for these doors:
sentences.n: 'Ille autem' leaves out the verb of speaking, 'but he (replied)', as so often. 'Tua… tua tristis imago' repeats the possessive for feeling: 'your image, your sad image'. Anchises's ghost had appeared to Aeneas in dreams (4.351–353) and on Sicily told him to come down to the underworld to meet him (5.722–740). 'Saepius' is 'quite often', 'again and again', the comparative used loosely. 'Occurrens' is 'meeting (me)'. 'Haec limina tendere' is 'to make for these thresholds', 'tendere' with an accusative of goal; 'adegit' is the perfect of 'adigo', 'drove', 'compelled'.

sentences.t: stant sale Tyrrheno classes.
sentences.l: stand on the Tyrrhenian salt the fleets.
sentences.i: my ships ride at anchor on the Tyrrhenian sea.
sentences.n: 'Stant' is 'stand', 'lie at anchor': the fleet is moored off Cumae, safe, as Anchises may wish to know. 'Sale Tyrrheno' is 'on the Tyrrhenian salt', 'sal' standing for the sea, the sea off the west coast of Italy. 'Classes' is a plural for the one fleet.

sentences.t:
Da iungere dextram,
da, genitor, teque amplexu ne subtrahe nostro.”
sentences.l:
Grant to join right hand,
grant, father, and yourself from our embrace do not withdraw.”
sentences.i: Give me your right hand to hold, father, give it, and do not slip away from my arms.”
sentences.n: 'Da iungere dextram' is 'grant (me) to join right hand (with yours)', the poetic 'do' with an infinitive, 'allow'. 'Da' is repeated with the vocative 'genitor' for urgency. 'Ne subtrahe' is 'ne' with the imperative again, as 'ne quaere' at 614, 'do not withdraw'. 'Amplexu… nostro' is an ablative of separation, 'from our (my) embrace', 'nostro' being a plural for the singular. The closing mark ends Aeneas's speech.

sentences.t: Sic memorans, largo fletu simul ora rigabat.
sentences.l: So speaking, with a flood of weeping at the same time his face he was watering.
sentences.i: As he said this, a flood of tears kept running down his face.
sentences.n: 'Sic memorans' is 'so speaking', 'memoro' being 'to speak of', 'to say'. 'Largo fletu' is 'with abundant weeping', an ablative of means. 'Simul' is 'at the same time', as he spoke. 'Ora rigabat' is 'was watering his face', the imperfect of something going on.

sentences.t:
Ter conatus ibi collo dare brachia circum,
ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago,
[par levibus ventis volucrique simillima somno.]
sentences.l:
Thrice he tried there to his neck to give arms around,
thrice in vain grasped from the hands escaped the image,
[equal to light winds and most like to a winged sleep.]
sentences.i: Three times he tried, there, to throw his arms around his father's neck; three times the image, grasped in vain, slipped from his hands, [as light as the breezes and most like a sleep that flies.]
sentences.n: These three lines are the same as 2.792–794, where Aeneas tries to embrace the ghost of his wife Creusa, and are rendered as there. Greenough brackets the third line here (702) as spurious, presumably as a repetition carried over from Book II, so it stands inside [ ] (in Book II he prints it plainly). 'Conatus (est)' is the perfect of the deponent 'conor', 'he tried'. 'Collo dare brachia circum' is a tmesis of 'circumdare', 'to put his arms around his neck', with 'collo' a dative; 'brachia' is Greenough's spelling here ('bracchia' in Book II). 'Comprensa' is 'grasped', from 'comprehendo', agreeing with 'imago'; 'manus' is an accusative plural, 'escaped the hands'. 'Par' and 'simillima' take the dative: 'equal to the light winds, most like to winged sleep', 'volucri' from 'volucer', 'winged', 'fleeting'. The model is Odysseus and the shade of his mother, who three times slips from his arms like a shadow or a dream (Odyssey 11.204–208).
